Fellow-Citizen
FEL-oh SIT-ih-zen
n.
Fellow + citizen; renders the Greek sumpolitēs, from sun- (with) + politēs (citizen, from polis, city)—a co-citizen of the same commonwealth.

📖 Biblical Definition

Fellow-citizen is Paul’s name in Ephesians 2:19 for the new political and covenantal identity of Gentile believers admitted to the commonwealth of God’s people in Christ: now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God. The verse stands at the climax of Paul’s argument across Ephesians 2 that the Gentiles who were once aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world, have been brought near by the blood of Christ. The dividing wall between Jew and Gentile has been broken down; Christ has made both one; He is Himself our peace; and the Gentile, by faith in Him, is no longer alien but fellow-citizen. The political imagery is precise. The believer is not merely a member of a religious club but a citizen of a real commonwealth, with the rights, duties, and identity that citizenship confers. Paul develops the theme elsewhere: for our conversation (our politeuma, citizenship, way-of-life-as-citizens) is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ (Phil 3:20). The saint’s primary citizenship is heavenly; his earthly nationality is real and meaningful but subordinate; and the fellow-citizens with whom he is most deeply united across every earthly border are the saints of every people, tribe, tongue, and nation who share his heavenly citizenship. Hebrews 11 echoes the theme: the patriarchs confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth and desired a better country, that is, an heavenly; Hebrews 12 announces the New Covenant saints have come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven. Fellow-citizenship therefore reorders the saint’s identity. His primary commonwealth is heaven; his fellow-citizens are the saints of every age and place; his earthly citizenships, while real and to be exercised faithfully, are penultimate. The Christian holds his earthly nationality with thanksgiving and exercises its duties faithfully; but he holds it as a sojourner whose deeper citizenship lies elsewhere and whose deepest unities cross every earthly border.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FELLOW-CITIZEN as one who is a citizen of the same state or community as another; in scripture, the Gentile believer admitted to the commonwealth of God’s people in Christ alongside the believing Jew (Eph 2:19).

expand to see more

FELLOW-CITIZEN, n. — One who is a citizen of the same state or community as another; one belonging to the same political society. Fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God (Eph 2:19).

CITIZEN, n. — 1. The native of a city, or an inhabitant who enjoys the freedom and privileges of the city in which he resides. 2. In a general sense, a native or permanent resident in a city or country. For our conversation is in heaven (Phil 3:20).

📖 Key Scripture

Ephesians 2:19 — "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God."

Philippians 3:20 — "For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ."

Hebrews 11:13-14 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country."

Hebrews 12:22-23 — "But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, To the general assembly and church of the firstborn..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The fellow-citizen doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the nationalist absolutization that locates the believer’s primary citizenship in his earthly nation and treats fellow-believers of other nations as secondary—and on the other by the rootless-cosmopolitan corruption that denies all meaningful earthly citizenship and locates the saint in a placeless universalism, against the apostolic balance.

expand to see more

Nationalist absolutization is the more visible contemporary corruption among believers in stable polities. The Christian’s primary citizenship is treated as his earthly nation, his deepest unities are with fellow-citizens of that earthly nation rather than with fellow-believers of other nations, and the apostolic claim that our conversation is in heaven is muted or postponed to the next life. The result is a believer whose nationalism is supreme and whose Christianity is colored by it—and a church that is in fact more deeply united by earthly nationality than by heavenly citizenship. The recovery is to put the apostolic order back. The believer is supremely a citizen of heaven; his deepest unities are with the saints of every nation; his earthly nationality is real, meaningful, and to be exercised faithfully, but penultimate. The black brother in another country, the Asian sister in a third, the European saint, the African believer—these are his fellow-citizens at the deepest level, and his earthly co-nationals who do not share his faith are not.

The opposite corruption is the rootless-cosmopolitan reading that denies all meaningful earthly citizenship and locates the saint in a placeless universalism. The believer treats his earthly nation as essentially indifferent, declines to honor his earthly fathers (in nation as well as family), refuses the duties of citizenship that providence has placed upon him, and dismisses the love of country as a form of idolatry. Scripture does not warrant this either. Paul retained his Jewishness, exercised his Roman citizenship when it served the gospel (Acts 22:25-29; 25:11), and never disowned his earthly identities even as he subordinated them. The believer is a sojourner with a heavenly citizenship and a real earthly citizenship to be exercised faithfully: paying his taxes, honoring his magistrates, loving his neighbors, contributing to the common good of his earthly polity, all while holding his earthly nationality with the open-handed thanksgiving of one whose deeper home lies elsewhere. Recover both ends. Refuse the nationalism that absolutizes earthly citizenship over heavenly, and refuse the cosmopolitanism that despises earthly citizenship altogether. The biblical pattern is real earthly citizenship subordinated to supreme heavenly citizenship—and the believer who holds both rightly is the believer Hebrews 11 commends: strangers and pilgrims on the earth who seek a better country.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sumpolitēs (fellow-citizen, Eph 2:19) and politeuma (citizenship, way-of-life-as-citizens, Phil 3:20)—the new political and covenantal identity of believers admitted to the commonwealth of God’s people in Christ, with the saints of every nation as fellow-citizens.

expand to see more

Greek sumpolitēs (G4847) — fellow-citizen (Eph 2:19).

Greek politeuma (G4175) — citizenship, commonwealth, way-of-life (Phil 3:20).

Greek politēs (G4177) — citizen (Acts 21:39, Paul as citizen of Tarsus).

Greek politeuō (G4176) — to live as a citizen (Acts 23:1; Phil 1:27).

Usage

"Fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God—Eph 2:19 reorders the believer’s identity around his new political-covenantal belonging in Christ."

"Our conversation (politeuma, citizenship) is in heaven—Phil 3:20 names the primary commonwealth."

"Nationalism absolutizes earthly citizenship; rootless cosmopolitanism despises it; biblical pattern holds real earthly citizenship subordinate to supreme heavenly citizenship."
